subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal
passage: Coach's note, Thursday. For three weeks two of my students, Sachin and Shreya, have been at the ground before six every morning. They made a deal: the one who skips pays for the other's chai. On Tuesday the cold was sharp, and Sachin's message read, “I'm not coming.” Shreya replied, “Then you're buying my chai and a very good story.” Twenty minutes later Sachin arrived at the gate, hands in sleeves, muttering. The pair jogged, then sat with tea in the grass. I did nothing except unlock the gate. Neither of them would have come alone on Tuesday, and they know it. I've noticed their warm-ups are getting longer and more careful, and they laugh at the start. — Coach

qa.q: What does the one who skips pay for?
What might Sachin have been feeling on the cold Tuesday?
qa.a: Reluctant to leave the warm bed, but also not wanting to let Shreya down.

qa.q: What else could the pair do to keep the habit going, and why?
qa.a: Agree on a backup plan for rain or very cold days, since weather is the easiest excuse to skip.

qa.q: How does the rule look to Shreya?
qa.a: Shreya finds that the deal makes skipping costly and turns the morning into something shared, which makes it easier to get up.

grounding: Two friends agree to meet at the ground at six, and the one who skips pays for the other's chai.

passage:
Monday, 6:50 am, written at the chai stall
Day 12 of the Rukmini–Gopika deal. Rules, for the record: we meet at the school ground gate at six every weekday, and whoever doesn't turn up buys the other a chai. (Gopika added, “and has to hear about it all day.”)
Today it was freezing and dark, and at 5:40 I lay in bed fully decided to skip. Then I pictured Gopika at the gate, stamping her feet, and me buying her chai at lunch while she told everyone. I got up.
She was there, obviously. We did three rounds of jogging, the stretches, and some sprints to the pole. Afterwards she said she'd nearly skipped too, but thought of me standing there alone.
Score so far: I owe her one chai (last Thursday, alarm didn't ring), she owes me none. Tomorrow I plan to keep it that way.
– Rukmini

qa.q: How many chais does Rukmini owe Gopika so far?
What was Rukmini feeling at 5:40 in the morning?
qa.a: Rukmini felt cold and unwilling, fully decided to skip, until picturing Gopika waiting brought a pang of guilt.

qa.q: What else could the two add to keep the deal going through winter?
qa.a: A back-up for the darkest mornings, like skipping rope in the school corridor, so the habit continues even when the ground is unusable.

qa.q: How does the deal look from Gopika's side?
qa.a: Gopika nearly skipped too but thought of Rukmini alone at the gate, so the deal works on both of them the same way.

grounding: Shows two friends meeting at the ground at six each morning, with a missed day costing a chai for the other, which makes skipping on cold days socially costly.

qa.q: At what time did Mridul reach the gate the first morning?
How did Reena feel about getting there first the next morning?

qa.q: What might keep the pair going if one of them falls ill?

qa.q: What does the deal mean for Mridul on a freezing morning?

grounding: Shows two friends meeting at six each morning where lateness costs a chai, making skipping on cold days socially costly.
